lessons.title: Swift Testing vs XCTest

quickCheck.prompt: What's the key difference between `#expect` and `#require` in Swift Testing?
quickCheck.explanation: `#require` throws when its condition fails, stopping the test immediately; `#expect` records the failure but lets the test keep running, so it can surface multiple issues in one run.

options.text: They are interchangeable aliases, since both macros were introduced purely as different spellings of the exact same underlying assertion mechanism
#require throws and stops the test on failure; #expect records the failure and continues
#require is only usable inside UI tests, and cannot be called from a plain unit test target that has no XCUIApplication involved anywhere
#expect stops the test on failure; #require records and continues

quickCheck.prompt: A test needs to verify that saving a profile calls the analytics logger exactly once. Which test double fits?
quickCheck.explanation: A spy records how many times it was called and with what arguments, so the test can assert on that interaction afterward — exactly what's needed here.

options.text: Spy

lessons.title: What's Worth Testing
lessons.body:
Not every line deserves a test, and a test that runs green isn't automatically telling you something useful. The judgment call is what to spend test-writing effort on.

## The test pyramid

- **Unit tests** — most of the suite; fast, isolated, one behaviour at a time
- **Integration tests** — fewer; check that real collaborators agree on a contract
- **End-to-end / UI tests** — fewest; slow, but the only layer catching wiring mistakes the others can't see

Invert the pyramid — most tests at the top — and the suite gets flaky enough that people stop trusting it, which is worse than having no suite at all.

## Behaviour, not implementation

A resilient assertion checks the outcome a caller cares about: a returned value, persisted state, a message sent. A brittle one checks a private detail, like whether a method ran or in what order — and fails on refactors that changed nothing observable.

## Flakiness has causes, not just symptoms

- Shared mutable state that leaks between tests — a singleton, a static, a leftover file
- Real wall-clock time or `sleep`, where a slower CI machine loses a race a local machine wins
- Order dependence — a test that only passes because an earlier test set something up

## Coverage is a flashlight, not a scoreboard

A covered line only means it executed, not that anything about it was checked. Coverage shows where you have *no* signal, not that tested branches are correct. Test at the seams — the boundaries where your code meets a dependency you don't own — since that's where wrong assumptions surface.

> KEY: A test earns its keep by failing when behaviour breaks and staying green when it doesn't — both halves matter.

quickCheck.prompt: Why is a test suite dominated by UI tests riskier than one shaped like a pyramid?
quickCheck.explanation: UI tests are slower and more environment-sensitive than unit tests, so a suite top-heavy with them becomes slow and flaky enough that people stop trusting — and eventually stop watching — its results.

options.text: Unit tests can't run in a CI environment, since CI runners are assumed to lack the frameworks needed to execute anything below the UI layer
UI tests can't catch integration bugs, since exercising the full app through its interface is defined as testing only isolated units in disguise
UI tests are slower and more environment-sensitive, so a top-heavy suite becomes slow and flaky enough to lose trust
UI tests require a paid CI plan to run

lessons.title: Testing Async and Concurrent Code

quickCheck.prompt: Why is `Task.sleep` inside a test considered a smell?
quickCheck.explanation: It waits on wall-clock time rather than an actual signal that the work finished, which makes the test slow and still leaves a race — one that usually, but not always, wins.

options.text: It can't be called from an async test function
It's deprecated API, and the toolchain refuses to compile any test target that still calls it anywhere in its source
It requires the test to run on the main actor, and using it anywhere off that actor is rejected outright by the compiler before the test can run
It makes the test slow and still leaves a race, since it waits on wall-clock time rather than a real completion signal

questions.prompt: You write `@Test(arguments: [1, 2, 3]) func rejectsInvalid(_ value: Int)`. What happens when this test runs?
questions.explanation: `@Test(arguments:)` runs the test body once per element in the collection and reports each run as an independent result, rather than folding every value into a single pass/fail.

options.text: It runs once and fails only if every element in the collection happens to fail the check inside the test body
It only compiles if value is declared as [Int], matching the element type of the arguments array exactly
It runs three times, once per element, each reported as its own pass/fail
It runs once, receiving the whole array as value

questions.prompt: How does shared setup in a Swift Testing `@Suite` compare to `setUp`/`tearDown` in an `XCTestCase`?
questions.explanation: Swift Testing instantiates the suite type fresh for every `@Test` it contains, so `init` and `deinit` naturally run before and after each test — the same per-test isolation `setUp`/`tearDown` gives an `XCTestCase`, without needing to override anything.

options.text: They're identical — both run once before all tests in the class, since Swift Testing's init and deinit are assumed to share a single instance across every @Test method in the suite rather than creating a fresh one per test
@Suite requires an explicit tearDown override to reset state, the same way an XCTestCase subclass must override tearDown to avoid leaking state between test runs across the whole suite
A @Suite type's init/deinit run once per test, since a fresh instance is created for each @Test, matching the effect of setUp/tearDown running before and after every method
@Suite setup can only run synchronously, unlike setUp

questions.prompt: Both tests in this suite pass every time, but a teammate expected `incrementTwice` to start from wherever `incrementOnce` left `counter` — as if the two tests shared one instance. Why doesn't that happen?
questions.explanation: Swift Testing constructs a new instance of the suite type for each `@Test` method, so stored properties like `counter` never carry state between tests — each test gets its own independent copy no matter what order they run in.

options.text: The tests only pass because they happen to run in declaration order, and Swift Testing is assumed to always execute test methods in exactly the order they were written
Swift Testing creates a fresh instance of CounterTests for every @Test, so counter starts over each time regardless of run order
@Suite runs its tests in alphabetical order, so incrementOnce always runs first and its state carries over correctly
counter is a var, so it's shared automatically across all tests declared in the struct, the same way a static property would be shared across every instance ever created

questions.prompt: In an `XCTestCase` subclass, when do `setUp()` and `tearDown()` run relative to a test method?
questions.explanation: XCTest calls `setUp()` immediately before each test method and `tearDown()` immediately after it, giving every test method fresh setup and cleanup rather than sharing state across the class.

options.text: Once before and after the whole class, the same way a Swift Testing suite's init and deinit are assumed to run only a single time for the entire type
setUp() runs before the first test only, and tearDown() likewise runs just once, after the very last test method in the class finishes
Only if the test method calls them explicitly
setUp() runs before every test method and tearDown() after every test method

questions.prompt: How does XCTest's default execution model compare to Swift Testing's when running tests within the same suite?
questions.explanation: XCTest executes a class's test methods one at a time unless parallel testing is explicitly enabled; Swift Testing parallelizes by default, so a suite that quietly relied on serial execution to avoid a data race can start failing intermittently once ported.

options.text: XCTest runs test methods within a class serially by default; Swift Testing runs tests concurrently by default, so tests touching shared mutable state can interfere where they wouldn't have under XCTest
Both run serially by default
Execution order makes no difference to either framework's results

Swift Testing runs tests serially; XCTest always runs in parallel, since XCTest was rebuilt around structured concurrency well before Swift Testing existed as a separate framework distributed with the toolchain

questions.prompt: A test passes every time you run it alone, but fails intermittently when the whole `XCTestCase` class runs. What's the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: A test that only fails in the company of others is a symptom of leaked state — a static, a singleton, or a `tearDown()` override that skips `super.tearDown()` — rather than a problem with the failing test itself.

options.text: The test is marked async incorrectly, since only a test function marked async is assumed capable of ever exhibiting order-dependent or intermittent failures tied to leftover state from another test
XCTest doesn't support more than one test method per class, which is why teams often split a single scenario across several small XCTestCase subclasses instead of combining them
The test file wasn't added to the test target
State left behind by an earlier test isn't being reset — often because an override of tearDown() forgot to call super.tearDown(), or a static/shared value isn't cleared

questions.prompt: Which test double just returns a pre-programmed answer when called, with no expectations about being called and no record kept of the call?
questions.explanation: A stub returns a canned value on request and doesn't care whether, or how many times, it's called — that's what separates it from a spy (which records calls) and a mock (which has expectations).

options.text: Dummy
Spy
Stub
Mock

questions.prompt: How does a spy differ from a mock as a test double?
questions.explanation: A spy is passive — it just remembers what was called so the test can check afterward — while a mock is active, carrying built-in expectations and failing on its own if the expected calls don't occur as scripted.

options.text: A spy records what happened to it — call count, arguments — so the test can assert on that afterward; a mock is pre-programmed with expected calls and fails the test itself if they don't happen
A spy replaces the real dependency; a mock only wraps it

A spy and a mock are the same thing under different names, since both ultimately exist to record every call made against the test double for later inspection by whatever assertion the test happens to make
A mock can only return Void; a spy can return any type

questions.prompt: This test checks that `store.saveWasCalled` and `store.saveCallCount` are correct, but never checks what was actually saved. What's the problem?
questions.explanation: This is the over-mocking smell: asserting on the fact of a call rather than its effect. A test that instead checked `store.savedProfile?.name == "Ada"` would verify the behaviour a caller actually cares about, and would survive an internal refactor of how saving is implemented.

options.text: Nothing — verifying the call happened is exactly what a test double is for, and asserting on call count is the standard way any test double is meant to be used, regardless of what the call actually did
It's coupled to implementation (that save was called, and how many times) instead of the outcome that matters — that the profile named "Ada" is what got persisted
The test needs an async version of save
MockProfileStore should be a Dummy instead, since a Dummy is the correct double whenever a test only cares about tracking how many times a method was invoked during a run

questions.prompt: A type calls `URLSession.shared` directly inside its methods. Compare that to a type that takes a `URLSession`-conforming protocol through its initializer, from a testability standpoint.
questions.explanation: Testability comes from having a seam — a point where the real implementation can be swapped for a test double. A hard-coded singleton reference has no such seam; injecting the dependency through `init`, typed as a protocol, gives tests exactly that point of substitution.

options.text: URLSession.shared is already a protocol, so no seam is needed
Both are equally testable, since URLSession can be mocked either way

The hard-coded version can only be tested by hitting the real network, since there's no seam to substitute a double; injecting the dependency through init gives the test a seam to hand in a stub or fake instead

Injecting the dependency makes the type slower at runtime, since resolving a protocol witness table costs measurably more than calling a concrete singleton directly every single time the method happens to run in production

questions.prompt: You need a unit test for `currentTemperature` that doesn't touch the network. What's the smallest change that makes this testable?
questions.explanation: The fix is to create a seam: define a narrow protocol for the networking call the type needs, inject a conformer through the initializer instead of reaching for the shared singleton, and let tests substitute a stub or fake that returns canned data with no network involved.

options.text: Make currentTemperature synchronous

Add a #if TESTING branch that returns a hardcoded value, so the compiler strips the real networking call out of the binary before it ever ships to the App Store, leaving nothing left to accidentally call in production
Mark the method @testable so tests can call it directly

Introduce a protocol that covers the fetching method it needs, inject an instance of it through the initializer instead of reaching for URLSession.shared, and hand the test a fake or stub conforming to that protocol

questions.prompt: Can a Swift Testing `@Test` function be `async`, and can `#expect` check the result of an `await`ed call directly?
questions.explanation: Swift Testing test functions can be declared `async throws` like any other async function, and `#expect` accepts an `await`ed expression directly, so there's no need for a separate expectation mechanism to test a value returned by async code.

options.text: No — async code must be tested with XCTestExpectation instead, since Swift Testing has no mechanism at all for awaiting anything inside a test function
Only if the function under test returns Void, since #expect cannot wrap an expression that produces any other kind of value
Yes — @Test functions can be marked async throws, and #expect can wrap an awaited expression inline
Yes, but only inside a @Suite, never as a top-level function

questions.prompt: What does this test verify?
questions.explanation: `confirmation(expectedCount:)` fails the test unless the passed-in `confirmed` closure is invoked exactly that many times before the confirmation body finishes — here, that's the mechanism for asserting both observers got notified exactly once each.

options.text: That Notifier supports at most two subscribers
That the confirmation closure runs exactly twice by the time confirmation returns — both subscribed observers are notified exactly once each when publish() is called
That publish() returns within a fixed time limit
That subscribe and publish are called in a specific order, since confirmation only passes when every closure runs before the outer function itself returns control back to the caller

questions.prompt: This test is flaky on CI but reliable locally. What's the most likely cause, and what's the better fix?
questions.explanation: A fixed sleep is a race with an arbitrary deadline: it passes as long as the real work finishes faster than the guess, which is exactly the kind of assumption that CI's variable load breaks. The fix is to wait on an actual completion signal from the code under test, not on wall-clock time.

options.text: Downloader needs to be marked @MainActor
The test guesses how long start() takes and waits a fixed 200ms; under CI load that guess is sometimes too short. Await a signal that the work actually finished instead of sleeping a fixed duration
Task.sleep isn't supported inside a Swift Testing @Test

CI machines run an older Swift version; pin the toolchain to the exact same version used on every developer's machine to keep the timing behaviour completely identical across every single environment involved

questions.prompt: Which of these is a typical cause of a flaky test?
questions.explanation: Flakiness usually traces back to state that isn't isolated per test — a singleton, a static variable, or a file left on disk from a previous run — so the outcome depends on what ran before, not just on the test's own logic.

options.text: The test is marked @Test instead of naming the function test...
Shared mutable state (a singleton, a static, a file on disk) that leaks between tests
The test asserts on a return value, since checking what a function returns is inherently less reliable than checking a side effect it produced
The test has a descriptive name, since a name that clearly states the expected behaviour is what actually makes a test flaky under load

questions.prompt: Some test suites deliberately randomize test execution order between runs. Why?
questions.explanation: A fixed run order can mask a hidden dependency between tests indefinitely, because the same lucky order runs every time. Randomizing the order turns that latent bug into a visible, if intermittent, failure — which is the point.

options.text: It surfaces order-dependent tests — ones that only pass because an earlier test happened to leave behind state they silently rely on — which a fixed order would hide indefinitely
Randomized order is a requirement of Swift Testing
It makes the suite run faster, since a randomized order lets independent tests execute without ever waiting on any fixed sequence between them at all, unlike a strictly serial run
It reduces the total number of assertions needed

questions.prompt: `testLogoutClearsToken` fails when run alone but passes when the full class runs. What's wrong?
questions.explanation: The static property makes the two tests silently dependent on each other's run order — `testLogoutClearsToken` only has a token to clear because a previous test happened to populate a shared static. Each test should arrange its own state instead of relying on another test as a side-effecting setup step.

options.text: XCTest always runs methods in declaration order, so this is actually safe, and the static var only ever gets read after it has already been written earlier in the run, so it happens to work out
Auth isn't marked Sendable
XCTAssertNil doesn't work correctly on optionals
The test depends on static var cachedToken, mutable state shared across test methods, being populated by testLoginStoresToken running first — an inter-test dependency through shared state

questions.prompt: In the classic test pyramid, which layer should make up the largest share of a suite?
questions.explanation: Unit tests sit at the base of the pyramid because they're fast and cheap to run, which is what lets a suite afford a lot of them; the slower layers above should shrink as you go up.

options.text: Manual tests, since a human clicking through the app by hand is assumed to be the fastest and cheapest layer to run on every single commit
Integration tests, since they sit in the middle of the pyramid and are assumed to be cheap enough to make up the bulk of any healthy test suite
Unit tests — fast and isolated, so you can afford a lot of them
End-to-end / UI tests, since they cover the most ground

questions.prompt: What makes an assertion 'resilient' rather than 'brittle'?
questions.explanation: A resilient assertion is anchored to observable behaviour, so an internal refactor that doesn't change that behaviour leaves the test green. Checking a private detail — like an exact call order — is what makes an assertion brittle.

options.text: It never fails, no matter what changes, since resilience is defined as an assertion that cannot possibly fail regardless of what the code under test actually does
It uses XCTAssertEqual instead of XCTAssertTrue, since the specific assertion macro chosen is what determines whether a check survives a refactor
It checks that a private method was called in a specific order
It checks an outcome the caller actually cares about — a return value, persisted state, a sent message — so it survives a refactor that preserves behaviour

questions.prompt: A test can assert either `#expect(cart.total == 42.0)` or `#expect(cart.applyDiscountWasCalled)`. Which is more resilient to an internal refactor of `Cart`, and why?
questions.explanation: The total is the behaviour a caller cares about; whether a particular private method fired is an implementation detail. A refactor that computes the same correct total through a different internal path breaks the call-tracking assertion for no behavioural reason.

options.text: They're equally resilient, since both assertions are assumed to be checking the exact same underlying fact about Cart, regardless of what each one literally reads
cart.total == 42.0 — it checks the outcome a caller of Cart actually observes, so it stays green through any refactor that keeps the total correct
applyDiscountWasCalled — it's more specific about what happened internally
Neither is resilient without a mock backing it, since an assertion cannot be considered trustworthy unless a mock object is verifying it behind the scenes

questions.prompt: This test fails whenever `Checkout` is refactored to apply shipping before tax, even though the final total is still correct either way. What's the underlying issue?
questions.explanation: If both call orders produce the same correct total, the order is an implementation detail, not a behaviour. Asserting on the recorded call sequence locks in one specific implementation and breaks on any refactor that changes it without changing what the caller actually sees.

options.text: The test is coupled to an implementation detail — the internal order of calls — rather than the outcome that matters, the final total; it should assert on sut.total(for: order)'s return value instead
The order genuinely matters for correctness, so the test is right to fail
MockPriceCalculator needs more test cases

Arrays aren't Equatable in Swift Testing, so calculator.calls would need to be compared element by element instead of with a single == check like the one written here, which would not compile as shown

questions.prompt: Compare a unit test of a view model's logic against a UI test that drives the same screen through `XCUIApplication`.
questions.explanation: Unit tests and UI tests catch different classes of bugs at very different costs: unit tests are fast and precise about logic but blind to wiring problems, while UI tests catch those wiring problems at the price of speed, stability, and a vaguer failure.

options.text: The unit test runs in milliseconds and isolates the logic, but can't catch a wiring mistake between the view and the model; the UI test catches that wiring but is slower and more environment-sensitive
UI tests can't assert on visible text on screen
Both take roughly the same amount of time to run

The UI test is strictly better since it exercises real user-facing behaviour, covering the view, the model, and the underlying network stack all in one single run without needing separate unit coverage

questions.prompt: A suite has 200 UI tests and 20 unit tests. It takes 40 minutes to run and fails about 1 run in 10 for reasons unrelated to real bugs. What's the most effective fix?
questions.explanation: An inverted pyramid — mostly UI tests — is both slow and flaky by nature, since UI tests are inherently more environment-sensitive. The fix is structural: move business-logic coverage down to fast unit tests, and keep the UI layer for the few flows that need true end-to-end confidence.

options.text: Retry every failing test automatically until it passes
Run the UI tests on faster build hardware
Delete the 20 unit tests since they add little coverage compared to the UI suite, which already exercises those same code paths end to end anyway without needing anything smaller
Push logic currently only exercised through the UI layer down into unit tests, and trim the UI suite to the handful of critical end-to-end flows it should actually own

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of relying heavily on snapshot tests for a view's UI?
questions.explanation: Snapshot tests are sensitive to any pixel difference, intentional or not, so a broad snapshot suite generates frequent, low-signal failures. The real risk is procedural: reviewers start re-recording snapshots reflexively instead of checking whether the new rendering is actually right.

options.text: They require a physical device to run

They're cheap to write but tend to fail on any incidental visual change — a font update, a spacing tweak — which trains people to re-record without actually reviewing whether the new output is correct

They can't detect any visual regressions at all, since a snapshot only records raw pixel data and has no independent way to compare one rendered image against another one without a human looking at both side by side
They remove the need for any other kind of test

questions.prompt: A snapshot test for a button has been green for a year. A designer points out the button's corner radius has always been wrong. Why didn't the snapshot test catch it?
questions.explanation: A snapshot test verifies stability against its own recorded baseline, not correctness against a spec. If the wrong output was what got recorded, the test will happily keep passing forever — it has no independent notion of what 'right' looks like.

options.text: Snapshot tests only detect a *change* from a recorded baseline — if the baseline itself was captured with the bug already present, there's nothing to compare against and the test stays green no matter how wrong the output is

The button must have been added after the snapshot was recorded, and the missing baseline meant the corner radius bug had nothing at all to be compared against until a human actually looked closely at the final rendered result
The test framework doesn't support asserting on corner radius
Snapshot tests only run on CI, never locally

questions.prompt: What does 100% code coverage on a module actually tell you?
questions.explanation: Coverage measures execution, not verification — a line can run with no assertion checking its result and still count as covered. It's most useful as a flashlight pointing at code with zero test signal, not as a score to maximize.

options.text: That every line executed at least once during the test run — it says nothing about whether the assertions checking that code were meaningful
That the module has no race conditions, since coverage tooling is defined as instrumenting every concurrent access path a module could ever take at runtime
That no further tests are needed for that module
That the module is bug-free, since a covered line is assumed to have already been checked against every input it could ever realistically receive

questions.prompt: This test interleaves several act-then-assert steps instead of one arrange, one act, one assert. What's the practical downside of writing it this way?
questions.explanation: This test conflates three separate scenarios under one test name and one pass/fail. Splitting it into three tests, each with one arrange, one act, one assert, gives a failure report that pinpoints exactly which scenario broke.

options.text: Inventory must be a class, not a struct, for this to work

It won't compile, since #expect can only appear once per test — Swift Testing enforces a single assertion per @Test function, rejecting a second #expect call inside the same test body at compile time before the test is ever even allowed to run

When one of the middle #expect calls fails, it's unclear whether the earlier state was ever correct — the test is really checking three scenarios crammed into one name, and a failure report doesn't say which one broke without reading the body
Nothing — this is the standard arrange-act-assert shape
